citeAs: Mihaylov, T., Clark, P., Khot, T., and Sabharwal, A. (2018). Can a Suit of Armor Conduct Electricity? A New Dataset for Open Book Question Answering. EMNLP 2018.
creator: Todor Mihaylov, Peter Clark, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal (Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence; Heidelberg University)
description: OpenBookQA is a multiple-choice question answering dataset modeled after open book exams. It consists of about 5957 4-way multiple-choice questions paired with a set of 1326 elementary-level science facts (the "open book"). Answering the questions requires combining a core science fact from the open book with broad common knowledge, probing multi-hop reasoning beyond simple retrieval or paraphrase matching.
name: OpenBookQA
rai:annotationsPerItem: 5 crowd-workers independently answered each question to verify answerability (step 6 of the pipeline).
rai:annotatorDemographics: Amazon Mechanical Turk workers from North America with a 'masters' level qualification. An in-house expert (Madeleine van Zuylen) provided additional annotation for Dev and Test questions.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human performance was estimated using the 5 independent annotations per question collected during the answerability verification step. Using Hoeffding's Inequality, the estimated human accuracy H(Q) is at least ~H(Q) − 3% with probability over 98.8%. On Dev and Test sets (500 questions each), this yields a conservative human accuracy estimate of ~92%. An additional assessment on 100 randomly chosen questions from each of Train, Dev, and Test gave 88.6%, 90.2%, and 91.6% respectively.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each crowd-worker was shown a random science fact f from F, asked to: (1) think of a second common fact k that combines with f to derive a new assertion; (2) convert the assertion into a question-answer pair and extend it into a 4-way multiple-choice question with 3 incorrect choices. The system then verified basic checks (exactly 4 choices, no negation words, uniform choice length). The question was fed to an IR solver and a word-association solver; if either answered correctly or the top-3 IR sentences were sufficient, the question was edited and retried. Five new crowd-workers then answered the question; if at least 4/5 answered correctly, it was kept. Answer choices were randomly shuffled to remove position bias. Dev and Test sets were further reviewed by an in-house expert.
rai:dataBiases: The paper explicitly acknowledges human bias in crowdsourced datasets: (1) Answer position bias — before shuffling, choice 'A' was the correct answer in 69% of questions. (2) Plausible answer bias — certain answer choices are inherently more plausible for science questions (e.g., 'flying cats' is unlikely to be correct), exploitable by a choice-only model achieving ~50% accuracy. (3) Odd-one-out bias — incorrect answer choices tend to be homogeneous or share properties uncharacteristic of the correct answer, since workers typically start with the correct answer and then generate three incorrect ones. (4) 21% of analyzed Train questions test a fact that doesn't necessarily require the original science fact used to generate them.
rai:dataCollection: Questions were created via a multi-stage crowdsourcing and partial expert filtering process. Workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk (from North America, with 'masters' level qualification) were shown a random science fact from the open book set F, asked to think of a second common fact, combine them into a new assertion, and convert it into a 4-way multiple-choice question. Questions were then filtered for hardness (must fool an IR solver and a word-association solver), answerability (at least 4 out of 5 crowd-workers must answer correctly), and de-biased by randomly shuffling answer choices. Dev and Test splits were further filtered by an in-house expert.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The core "open book" facts F are a subset of 1326 facts drawn from the WorldTree corpus (Jansen et al., 2018), specifically from the 2287 WorldTree facts marked as "central" in at least one explanation, further filtered to those general enough to be applicable to multiple situations. Questions were generated by crowd-workers based on these facts.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web API, Others
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset has several acknowledged limitations: (1) The additional facts K provided by crowd-workers are often incomplete, over-complete, or only distantly related to the question, and should not be treated as gold additional facts. (2) 21% of analyzed questions test a fact that does not necessarily require the original science fact used to generate them. (3) Simple neural baselines can exploit annotation artifacts (plausible answer bias, odd-one-out bias) to achieve ~50% accuracy without understanding the question. (4) Even with oracle facts (f+k), accuracy is only ~76%, far below human performance of ~92%, indicating non-trivial reasoning challenges remain.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The open book facts F were filtered from 2287 WorldTree "central" facts down to 1326 that appear general enough to be applicable to multiple situations. Questions were filtered using: (1) automatic checks for exactly 4 answer choices, absence of negation words, and uniform answer choice length; (2) hardness filter requiring that neither an IR solver nor a word-association solver answers correctly and the top-3 IR retrieved sentences are insufficient; (3) answerability filter requiring at least 4/5 crowd-workers to answer correctly; (4) answer choice shuffling to remove position bias; (5) expert review for Dev and Test splits. Overall, 8140 questions were collected and 2183 were discarded in the answerability filtering step.
rai:dataSocialImpact: OpenBookQA is intended to advance research on question answering systems that require multi-hop reasoning and integration of external knowledge, moving beyond simple retrieval and paraphrase matching. The dataset highlights the large gap between current NLP systems (~50%) and human performance (~92%), motivating further research on knowledge retrieval and reasoning for AI systems.
rai:dataUseCases: Open book question answering requiring multi-hop reasoning; evaluating systems that combine a provided set of core science facts with broad external common knowledge; benchmarking QA systems on elementary-level science questions; studying knowledge retrieval and reasoning in NLP systems.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: An IR solver (Clark et al., 2016) and a word-association based solver (Turney, 2017) were used during question generation to filter out questions that could be answered by retrieval or association-based methods. TfIdfVectorizer (from scikit-learn) was used for knowledge retrieval in baseline models.
